prompt: Fix positive integers $k$ and $d$. Prove that for all sufficiently large odd positive integers $n$, the digits of the base-$2n$ representation of $n^k$ are all greater than $d$.
answer: For odd $n$ and $1 \le \ell \le k$, the remainder of $n^k$ modulo $(2n)^\ell$ is $c\,n^\ell$ with $c$ odd, so it is at least $n^\ell$; hence the $\ell$-th digit from the right is at least $\lfloor n/2^{\ell-1}\rfloor > d$ once $n \ge (d+1)2^{k-1}$.

prompt: Let $n > k \ge 1$ be integers. Let $P(x) \in \mathbb R[x]$ be a polynomial of degree $n$ with no repeated roots and $P(0) \ne 0$. Suppose that for any real numbers $a_0, \dots, a_k$ such that the polynomial $a_kx^k + \dots + a_1x + a_0$ divides $P(x)$, the product $a_0a_1\dots a_k$ is zero. Prove that $P(x)$ has a nonreal root.
answer: If all roots were real, take $k+1$ of them: the $k+1$ degree-$k$ products of $k$ of these roots each have a zero middle coefficient, two share a position, and then the product of the remaining $k-1$ roots has two consecutive zero coefficients — impossible for a polynomial with distinct real roots (Rolle).

solutions.title: Pigeonhole on zero coefficients, then Rolle
solutions.body:
Suppose, for contradiction, that all roots of $P$ are real. They are distinct and nonzero. Choose $k + 1$ of them, $\rho_1, \dots, \rho_{k+1}$ (possible since $n \ge k+1$), and for each $i$ let
$$R_i(x) = \prod_{j \ne i}(x - \rho_j),$$
a monic polynomial of degree $k$ dividing $P$. By hypothesis some coefficient of $R_i$ is zero. Its leading coefficient is $1$ and its constant coefficient is $\pm\prod_{j\ne i}\rho_j \ne 0$, so the zero coefficient is at one of the positions $1, 2, \dots, k-1$. If $k = 1$ there are no such positions — contradiction already. Otherwise, there are $k + 1$ polynomials and only $k - 1$ positions, so by pigeonhole two of them, say $R_1$ and $R_2$, have zero coefficient of $x^t$ for the same $t$ with $1 \le t \le k - 1$.

**Two consecutive zero coefficients.** Let
$$Q(x) = \prod_{j=3}^{k+1}(x - \rho_j) = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} b_jx^j, \qquad b_{k-1} = 1,$$
and $b_{-1} = 0$. Then $R_1 = (x - \rho_2)Q$ and $R_2 = (x - \rho_1)Q$, whose $x^t$-coefficients are $b_{t-1} - \rho_2 b_t$ and $b_{t-1} - \rho_1 b_t$. Both vanish and $\rho_1 \ne \rho_2$, so $b_t = b_{t-1} = 0$, with $0 \le t - 1 < t \le k - 1$. Since $b_{k-1} = 1$, in fact $t \le k - 2$ (so for $k = 2$ we already have a contradiction).

**Lemma.** A real polynomial $F$ of degree $d$ with $d$ distinct real roots has no two consecutive zero coefficients below its leading term.

*Proof.* By Rolle's theorem, between consecutive roots of $F$ lies a root of $F'$, so $F'$ has $d - 1$ distinct real roots; as $\deg F' = d - 1$, these are all its roots and they are simple. Repeating, every derivative $F^{(s)}$ with $s < d$ has $d - s$ distinct, simple real roots. If the coefficients $c_s, c_{s+1}$ of $x^s, x^{s+1}$ in $F$ vanish (with $s + 1 < d$), then $F^{(s)}(0) = s!\,c_s = 0$ and $F^{(s+1)}(0) = (s+1)!\,c_{s+1} = 0$, so $0$ is a multiple root of $F^{(s)}$ — contradiction. $\square$

$Q$ has degree $k - 1$ and the distinct real roots $\rho_3, \dots, \rho_{k+1}$, and $b_{t-1} = b_t = 0$ with $t < k - 1$. This contradicts the lemma. Hence $P$ has a nonreal root. ∎

prompt:
Alice the architect and Bob the builder play a game. First, Alice chooses two points $P$ and $Q$ in the plane and a subset $S$ of the plane, which are announced to Bob. Next, Bob marks infinitely many points in the plane, designating each a city. He may not place two cities within distance at most one unit of each other, and no three cities he places may be collinear. Finally, roads are constructed between the cities as follows: each pair $A, B$ of cities is connected with a road along the line segment $AB$ if and only if the following condition holds:

> For every city $C$ distinct from $A$ and $B$, there exists $R \in S$ such that $\triangle PQR$ is directly similar to either $\triangle ABC$ or $\triangle BAC$.

Alice wins the game if (i) the resulting roads allow for travel between any pair of cities via a finite sequence of roads and (ii) no two roads cross. Otherwise, Bob wins. Determine, with proof, which player has a winning strategy.

solutions.title: Make the roads the Gabriel graph
solutions.body:
**Alice's choice.** Alice picks any two distinct points $P, Q$ and lets $S$ be the set of points outside the closed disk with diameter $PQ$. For $R$ not on line $PQ$, $R \in S$ if and only if $\angle PRQ < 90^\circ$.

**What the roads are.** Let $A, B, C$ be cities; they are not collinear. There is exactly one point $R$ with $\triangle PQR$ directly similar to $\triangle ABC$, and one with $\triangle PQR$ directly similar to $\triangle BAC$; in both cases $R \notin PQ$ and $\angle PRQ = \angle ACB$. So the condition for $C$ holds if and only if $\angle ACB < 90^\circ$, i.e. $C$ lies outside the closed disk with diameter $AB$. Hence:

> $A$ and $B$ are joined by a road if and only if no other city lies in the closed disk with diameter $AB$.

We show that for **every** admissible set of cities (no three collinear, all distances greater than $1$), this graph is connected and has no crossing roads.

**No crossings.** Suppose roads $AC$ and $BD$ cross at a point interior to both (four distinct cities). Then $ABCD$ is a convex quadrilateral with diagonals $AC$ and $BD$. Its angles sum to $360^\circ$, so one of them is at least $90^\circ$; say $\angle DAB \ge 90^\circ$ (the other vertices are analogous). Then $A$ lies in the closed disk with diameter $BD$, so $BD$ is not a road — contradiction.

**Connected.** Suppose not, and pick cities $p_1, q_1$ in different components; let $\delta_1 = |p_1q_1|$. Since $p_1q_1$ is not a road, some city $r$ lies in the closed disk with diameter $p_1q_1$, so $\angle p_1rq_1 \ge 90^\circ$ and
$$|p_1r|^2 + |rq_1|^2 \le |p_1q_1|^2.$$
The city $r$ is in a different component from at least one of $p_1, q_1$; call that one $p_2$ and set $q_2 = r$, $\delta_2 = |p_2q_2|$. The other distance is greater than $1$, so $\delta_2^2 < \delta_1^2 - 1$. Repeating forever gives cities $p_i, q_i$ in different components with $\delta_i^2 < \delta_1^2 - (i - 1)$, which is negative for large $i$ — contradiction.

So whatever Bob does, the roads connect all cities without crossings: **Alice** has a winning strategy. ∎

*Remark.* This road network is known as the Gabriel graph of the cities.

prompt: Let $H$ be the orthocenter of an acute triangle $ABC$, let $F$ be the foot of the altitude from $C$ to $AB$, and let $P$ be the reflection of $H$ across $BC$. Suppose that the circumcircle of triangle $AFP$ intersects line $BC$ at two distinct points $X$ and $Y$. Prove that $CX = CY$.
answer: With $Q$ the antipode of $B$ on the circumcircle, the midpoint $M$ of $QC$ is the center of $(AFP)$ ($APCQ$ is an isosceles trapezoid, and $MN \perp AB$ for the midpoint $N$ of $AF$); since $MC \perp BC$, $C$ is the midpoint of $XY$.

prompt:
Find all positive integers $k$ such that: for every positive integer $n$, the sum
$$\binom n0^k + \binom n1^k + \dots + \binom nn^k$$
is divisible by $n + 1$.
answer: All even $k$. Odd $k$ fails at $n = 2$. For even $k$: if $p^e \parallel n+1$, then $\binom ni \equiv \pm\binom{(n+1)/p - 1}{\lfloor i/p\rfloor} \pmod{p^e}$, so $S(n) \equiv p\,S\!\left(\frac{n+1}p - 1\right) \pmod {p^e}$; induct.

solutions.title: Reduce $n+1$ to $(n+1)/p$ modulo $p^e$
solutions.body:
Let $S(n) = \sum_{i=0}^n \binom ni^k$.

**$k$ must be even.** For $n = 2$: $S(2) = 1 + 2^k + 1 \equiv 2 + (-1)^k \pmod 3$, which is $0$ only for even $k$.

**Even $k$ works.** Fix an even $k$. We prove $(n+1) \mid S(n)$ for all $n \ge 0$ by strong induction ($S(0) = 1$ is divisible by $1$). Let $n \ge 1$; it suffices to show $p^e \mid S(n)$ for each prime power $p^e$ exactly dividing $n + 1$ ($e \ge 1$). Put $n' = \frac{n+1}{p} - 1$, so $0 \le n' < n$ and $p^{e-1}$ exactly divides $n' + 1$.

**Lemma.** For $0 \le i \le n$, $\binom ni \equiv \pm\binom{n'}{\lfloor i/p\rfloor} \pmod{p^e}$.

*Proof.* Write $\binom ni = \prod_{j=1}^i \frac{n + 1 - j}{j}$ and split the factors by whether $p \mid j$.
- If $j = pj'$, the factor is $\frac{n+1-pj'}{pj'} = \frac{n' + 1 - j'}{j'}$; over $j' = 1, \dots, \lfloor i/p\rfloor$ these multiply to $\binom{n'}{\lfloor i/p\rfloor}$.
- Let $U = \prod j$ and $V = \prod (n + 1 - j)$ over $1 \le j \le i$ with $p \nmid j$, and let $u$ be the number of such $j$.

So $U\binom ni = V\binom{n'}{\lfloor i/p\rfloor}$ as integers. Since $p^e \mid n+1$, $V \equiv \prod(-j) = (-1)^u U \pmod{p^e}$. As $U$ is coprime to $p$, we may cancel it: $\binom ni \equiv (-1)^u\binom{n'}{\lfloor i/p\rfloor} \pmod{p^e}$. $\square$

Since $k$ is even, the sign disappears: $\binom ni^k \equiv \binom{n'}{\lfloor i/p\rfloor}^k \pmod{p^e}$. The $n + 1 = p(n'+1)$ indices $i$ split into the blocks $\lfloor i/p\rfloor = j$ for $j = 0, \dots, n'$, each of size $p$. Hence
$$S(n) \equiv p\sum_{j=0}^{n'}\binom{n'}{j}^k = p\,S(n') \pmod{p^e}.$$
By the induction hypothesis $(n'+1) \mid S(n')$, so $p^{e-1} \mid S(n')$ and $p^e \mid p\,S(n')$. Thus $p^e \mid S(n)$. Doing this for every prime power exactly dividing $n+1$ gives $(n+1) \mid S(n)$.

**Answer:** exactly the even positive integers $k$. ∎

prompt: Let $m$ and $n$ be positive integers with $m \ge n$. There are $m$ cupcakes of different flavors arranged around a circle and $n$ people who like cupcakes. Each person assigns a nonnegative real number score to each cupcake, depending on how much they like the cupcake. Suppose that for each person $P$, it is possible to partition the circle of $m$ cupcakes into $n$ groups of consecutive cupcakes so that the sum of $P$'s scores of the cupcakes in each group is at least $1$. Prove that it is possible to distribute the $m$ cupcakes to the $n$ people so that each person $P$ receives cupcakes of total score at least $1$ with respect to $P$.
answer: Fix one person's $n$ arcs and use Hall's theorem to find a nonempty group of people matched to some of her arcs such that nobody else likes any matched arc; give out those arcs, delete them, and observe each other person's partition merges into one with one fewer group, each still worth $\ge 1$; induct on $n$.

solutions.title: Hall's theorem plus a deletion induction
solutions.body:
Say a person *likes* a set of cupcakes if its total score for that person is at least $1$. We prove the statement by induction on $n$ (for every $m \ge n$). For $n = 1$, give all cupcakes to the single person; her one group is the whole circle.

Let $n \ge 2$. Pick any person, Pip, and fix her partition into $n$ arcs. Form a bipartite graph $G$ between the $n$ people and Pip's $n$ arcs, joining a person to an arc she likes. Pip is joined to every arc.

**Hall's theorem.** In a bipartite graph, the people can all be matched to distinct neighbors if and only if every set $B$ of people has at least $|B|$ neighbors.

**Peeling off bad sets.** Start with $X_0$ = all people and $Y_0$ = all arcs. Given $X_i, Y_i$ with $|Y_i| \ge |X_i|$: if the graph $G[X_i, Y_i]$ has a matching saturating $X_i$, stop. Otherwise, by Hall there is $B_i \subseteq X_i$ with fewer than $|B_i|$ neighbors in $Y_i$; set $X_{i+1} = X_i \setminus B_i$ and $Y_{i+1} = Y_i \setminus N(B_i)$. Then $|Y_{i+1}| - |X_{i+1}| > |Y_i| - |X_i| \ge 0$. Pip is never removed: if Pip $\in B_i$, then $N(B_i) \cap Y_i = Y_i$, so $|Y_i| < |B_i| \le |X_i|$, which is false. The process stops (the sets shrink) at some $X_t \ni$ Pip with a matching of $X_t$ into a set $Y^* \subseteq Y_t$ of $|X_t|$ arcs.

**Key property.** Every person $q \notin X_t$ was removed in some $B_i$, together with all of her neighbors in $Y_i$; since $Y^* \subseteq Y_t \subseteq Y_{i+1}$, **$q$ likes none of the arcs in $Y^*$.**

Give each person of $X_t$ her matched arc. If $X_t$ is everybody, we are done. Otherwise let $n' = n - |X_t|$, so $1 \le n' < n$, and delete the cupcakes of the arcs in $Y^*$; the remaining cupcakes, in their circular order, form a new circle.

**The remaining people still have good partitions.** Fix $q \notin X_t$ and her partition into $n$ groups (cut at $n$ of the gaps between neighboring cupcakes). Delete the arcs of $Y^*$ one at a time; each one, say $A$, is a block of consecutive cupcakes in the current circle that $q$ does not like. Then at most one of $q$'s cuts lies strictly inside $A$: two such cuts would enclose a whole group of $q$ inside $A$, and since scores are nonnegative, $A$ would be worth at least $1$ to $q$.
- If one cut lies inside $A$, then $A \subseteq G_1 \cup G_2$ for the two groups $G_1, G_2$ meeting at that cut.
- If no cut lies inside $A$, then $A \subseteq G_1$ for one group; let $G_2$ be a neighboring group (it exists as $q$ currently has at least $2$ groups).

Replace $G_1, G_2$ by $(G_1 \cup G_2) \setminus A$. This is a block of consecutive cupcakes in the new circle, and its score is at least $1 + 1 - (\text{score of } A) > 1 + 1 - 1 = 1$. The other groups do not meet $A$ and are unchanged. So after deleting $A$, $q$ has a partition of the new circle into one fewer group, each worth at least $1$. Before the $j$-th deletion she has $n - j + 1 \ge n' + 1 \ge 2$ groups, so this always applies. After all $|X_t|$ deletions, $q$ has a partition of the remaining circle into $n'$ groups that she likes (in particular at least $n'$ cupcakes remain).

By the induction hypothesis the $n'$ remaining people can share the remaining cupcakes so that each gets total score at least $1$. Together with the arcs given to $X_t$, everyone is satisfied. ∎
